note_tweet.text:
Privacy in the Age of AI - Is Privacy truly dead?

Unbelievable in less than a year we've gone from OpenClaw to now multiple personal AI agent platforms namely - Grokbot, OpenAI Dots, Meta Muse and Google Gemini/Spark just to name a few.

In order for these to be useful you need to feed it info, they are very data hungry and it's the "context" paired with the power of AI that makes them so useful.

But what happens when they start harvesting more data than what you thought?

Meta's Muse builds and maintains detailed “pages” or profiles on friends, family, colleagues, partners, and others mentioned in those communications—even people who never signed up for Muse or consented to any data sharing. These profiles can include relationship history, preferences, shared interests, and other details extracted from emails, chats, contacts, and photos. Muse is instructed to update them roughly hourly using the user’s data (plus public information).

I'd argue this extends surveillance to non-consenting third parties: your consent covers your data, but not the information about others sitting in your inbox or messages. Meta’s response is that this context is needed for the agent to be useful which is probably true.

Interestingly from my quick research, none of the other personal agent platforms go to this level of data harvesting. The cynic in me thinks this is what happens when your personal agent is built by a company who's business is to sell advertising. But the practical implication is Meta is right, the more data you give your personal agent the more useful it will be.

So what's it going to be?

So now since Grok @bot supports + addressing I've enabled a cool little thing.

I subscribe to a lot of newsletters, some of them sometimes have stuff that interest me, sometimes they don't. 

Manually sifting through them is a mega waste of time. 

So I created a +newsletter email address, and a newsletter bot. 

In my mail client (I use Fastmail but it works in Gmail), I forward ANY emails with the word 'unsubscribe' in it to the +newsletter email address. 

Then the newsletter bot gives me an hourly summary of all the emails that came through, highlights things I might be interested in and can delve deeper if I ask it. 

Saves me hours and hours.

note_tweet.text:
The most obvious way to use Grokbot = Your own custom newsletter sent to your email:

I easily within 1 day setup an elaborate newsletter with Grokbot by just explaining to it to link my email, and to include so and so many stories about [Topic] and then to organize these topics and stories and send it to my email everyday based on the previous 24 hours. 

Already it is the best newsletter by far since it is so personalized and at any time I can make tweaks to it in my “Newsletter” Grok bot —I can adjust topics or add new sections or features, etc... You can source things from X, Youtube, and elsewhere (it seems Reddit and some places block access which is annoying but maybe Elon will fix this…), 

Grokbot can even pick up stories from other newsletters, and because of this you can source only those that you want from them instead of having to read what you’re not interested in.

And for each story I have it provide a source link, top X posts about the story, and X search as little clickable links—which allows me to search the topic on X by clicking a button next to each story. 

Each story is stated in a one-two line summary overview in simple speech and if I want to read or learn more I can click the source, top X post, or search buttons.

Side note: I learned in order to create more than one Grokbot you just ask any Grokbot to create a new one and name it, and it creates it and then you can access it on the left area of the Grok app on your phone (each named Grokbot Chat is here). 

Then you can chat with your various bots in order to create tasks for it to do periodically. 

You just talk to it in natural language explaining what you want and it makes it for you or adjusts it for you, it’s that simple.

• Subscription Auditor: scans receipts in your email and any bank statement you share to show what you're really paying for
